metadata.title: Research on the influence of teachers’ ICT Capacity on classroom teaching quality: An intermediary model based on self-efficacy

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for the Shanghai region (OECD, 2018) and reports an analytic sample of 2945 teachers after excluding missing values. The manuscript does not report the use of TALIS sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife), nor does it name any weight variable (such as TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because the analysis is based on regression/mediation/quantile/threshold models rather than IEA PV scaling, the paper does not describe any PV-specific weighting; however, TALIS is collected under a complex survey design, so standard practice would be to apply TALIS sampling weights when estimating population-representative effects. Given the absence of explicit weight discussion, the safest interpretation is that weights were not incorporated into the reported coefficients and variance decompositions.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are Likert-scale composite scores from TALIS (teacher self-reported classroom teaching quality dimensions) rather than cognitive achievement scores generated via PVs. Missing data handling is described as removing missing values to obtain the final valid teacher sample, so a PV/missing-data strategy for achievement PVs is not relevant here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 teacher data for the Shanghai region of China. The authors screened for data responsiveness on the variables needed for teachers’ ICT capacity, teachers’ self-efficacy, and classroom teaching quality, and then removed cases with missing values to obtain the final analytic sample of 2945 valid teachers.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) — teacher survey (junior high teachers), classroom teaching quality (overall)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple linear regression: ICT capacity coefficient = 0.297 (SE=0.014), p<0.01; R-squared = 0.128; N=2945. Quantile regression: ICT capacity coefficients at quantiles 0.1/0.3/0.5/0.7/0.9 = 0.203/0.265/0.245/0.345/0.372 (all p<0.01 except where noted); Threshold regression: ICT capacity effects = 0.201 (ICT≤0.820), 0.280 (0.820<ICT≤0.890), 0.357 (ICT>0.890), all p<0.01.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey the study leveraged Teachers’ ICT capacity along with Age group, Teaching experience (years), Gender, and Educational qualification to model Classroom teaching quality (overall), finding that ICT capacity had a significant positive association (e.g., coefficient 0.297, p<0.01) and stronger gains at higher teaching-quality quantiles (up to 0.372) with a double-threshold pattern (0.201/0.280/0.357 across ICT capacity intervals). This indicates that strengthening teachers’ ICT capacity—especially for teachers already performing at mid-to-high levels—may improve classroom teaching quality, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) — teacher survey (junior high teachers), classroom teaching quality (sub-dimension: clear teaching)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple linear regression: ICT capacity coefficient = 0.297 (SE=0.015), p<0.01; R-squared = 0.132; N=2945. Shapley decomposition: ICT capacity Shapley value = 85.43% (estimated coefficient 0.06866).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey the study leveraged Teachers’ ICT capacity along with Gender, Age group, Teaching experience (years), and Educational qualification to model Clear teaching, finding that ICT capacity was a significant positive predictor (coefficient 0.297, p<0.01) and accounted for the largest share of explained variance via Shapley decomposition (85.43%). This indicates that ICT capacity development is likely to be a high-leverage lever for improving the clarity of instruction, though the study’s regression-based approach does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) — teacher survey (junior high teachers), classroom teaching quality (sub-dimension: cognitive mobilization)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple linear regression: ICT capacity coefficient = 1.365 (SE=0.064), p<0.01; R-squared = 0.146; N=2945. Shapley decomposition: ICT capacity Shapley value = 97.40% (estimated coefficient 0.14184).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey the study leveraged Teachers’ ICT capacity along with Age group, Teaching experience (years), Gender, and Educational qualification to model Cognitive mobilization, finding that ICT capacity had the strongest positive effect among the teaching-quality dimensions (coefficient 1.365, p<0.01) and dominated variance contribution (97.40% Shapley share). This indicates that policies and professional development that build teachers’ ICT capacity may most effectively enhance students’ cognitive engagement and active participation, while causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional associations.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) — teacher survey (junior high teachers), classroom teaching quality (sub-dimension: classroom management)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple linear regression: ICT capacity coefficient = 0.697 (SE=0.082), p<0.01; R-squared = 0.033; N=2945. Shapley decomposition: ICT capacity Shapley value = 80.03% (estimated coefficient 0.02652).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey the study leveraged Teachers’ ICT capacity along with Teaching experience (years), Age group, Gender, and Educational qualification to model Classroom management, finding that ICT capacity had a significant positive association (coefficient 0.697, p<0.01) but the smallest effect size among the three sub-dimensions and a lower variance contribution than cognitive mobilization (80.03% Shapley share). This indicates that ICT capacity alone may be insufficient to substantially strengthen classroom management practices, suggesting that complementary training in instructional organization and discipline management may be needed.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) — teacher survey (junior high teachers), mediation pathway
main_findings.target_variable: Mediation: ICT capacity → teachers’ self-efficacy → classroom teaching quality
main_findings.performance_metrics: Mediation models: ICT capacity → classroom teaching quality (direct) coefficient = 0.297 (SE=0.014), p<0.01; ICT capacity → self-efficacy coefficient = 0.396 (SE=0.017), p<0.01; self-efficacy → classroom teaching quality coefficient = 0.221 (SE=0.015), p<0.01. Bootstrap (5000 resamples): indirect effect = 0.088 with 95% CI [0.074, 0.102] (percentile) and [0.093, 0.127] (bias-corrected), excluding zero; direct effect CI excludes zero.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey the study leveraged Teachers’ ICT capacity and Teachers’ self-efficacy (plus Age group, Teaching experience (years), and Gender) to test a mediation pathway to classroom teaching quality, finding a significant partial mediation effect with an indirect effect of 0.088 (95% CI [0.074, 0.102]) and a significant direct effect remaining after accounting for self-efficacy. This indicates that ICT capacity improvements may raise teaching quality partly by strengthening teachers’ self-efficacy, implying that professional development should combine technical training with confidence-building and supportive implementation conditions, while recognizing the cross-sectional design.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for the Shanghai region of China (N=2945 teachers after excluding missing values) to examine how teachers’ ICT capacity relates to classroom teaching quality and whether self-efficacy mediates this relationship. Using multiple linear regression, Shapley value decomposition, quantile regression (quantiles 0.1/0.3/0.5/0.7/0.9), and Hansen-style threshold regression, the authors find that ICT capacity has a significant positive association with overall classroom teaching quality (coefficient 0.297, p<0.01) and with all three sub-dimensions, with the largest effect on cognitive mobilization (1.365, p<0.01). Heterogeneity appears across quantiles (ICT effects up to 0.372) and a double-threshold pattern emerges (0.201/0.280/0.357 across ICT capacity intervals). Mediation tests show partial mediation via self-efficacy (indirect effect 0.088; 95% CIs exclude zero). Limitations include cross-sectional data and no explicit reporting of TALIS sampling-weight use, so population-representative inference and causal claims are constrained.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper uses regression-based models and mediation/heterogeneity techniques, it does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive algorithms (no ML learners such as Random Forest/XGBoost/SVM/NN are reported). Therefore, the ML technique fields are left empty, and the extraction focuses on the statistical relationships reported for TALIS 2018 teacher outcomes.
